flashcards.definition: The SI amount-of-substance unit corresponding to $$6.022\times10^{23}$$ specified entities (atoms, molecules, or ions).
The mass of $$1$$ mole of a substance, expressed in $$\text{g mol}^{-1}$$, numerically equal to the formula mass in $$\text{u}$$.
An analytical technique that ionizes particles and separates them by $$m/z$$ to reveal isotopic composition and relative abundances.
Atoms of the same element that contain identical numbers of protons but different numbers of neutrons, leading to distinct masses.
The weighted mean of the masses of naturally occurring nuclides of an element, using fractional abundances as weights.

multipleChoice.questionText: Element X has two stable nuclides: $$62.93\ \text{u}$$ at $$69.1\%$$ abundance and $$64.93\ \text{u}$$ at $$30.9\%$$ abundance. What is the average atomic mass of X?
A mass spectrum of element Q shows two prominent peaks at $$m/z=70$$ and $$m/z=72$$ with relative intensities of approximately 3:1. What is the approximate percent abundance of the heavier nuclide?

fillInTheBlank.questionText: One mole of silicon contains ______ atoms.
In a typical mass spectrum, the horizontal axis is labeled ______.

flashcards.definition: Arrangement of electrons among atomic orbitals described by notation such as $$1s^22s^22p^6\ldots$$ and determined by the aufbau principle, the Pauli exclusion principle, and Hund’s rule.
Within a set of degenerate orbitals, electrons occupy different orbitals with parallel spins before pairing occurs.
A technique that measures the kinetic energies of ejected electrons to determine their binding energies, revealing subshell structure and relative electron counts.
The net positive attraction experienced by a given electron in a multi-electron atom, approximated by $$Z_{\text{eff}}=Z-S$$ where $$S$$ accounts for shielding by other electrons.
The minimum energy required to remove the outermost electron from a gaseous atom in its ground state, typically reported per mole of atoms.

multipleChoice.questionText: A PES for a neutral atom shows three groups of peaks whose relative areas are 2 (highest binding energy), 2 (intermediate), and 1 (lowest). The highest-binding-energy group corresponds to the $$1s$$ subshell, followed by $$2s$$, then $$2p$$. Which element best matches these data?
Which statement best explains why $$IE_1(\text{O})<IE_1(\text{N})$$ despite oxygen’s greater nuclear charge?
options: In oxygen, one $$2p$$ orbital is doubly occupied, increasing electron–electron repulsion and lowering the energy needed to remove an electron.
Oxygen has a smaller atomic radius than nitrogen, reducing shielding and making electron removal easier.
Oxygen has a lower nuclear charge than nitrogen, so its valence electron is less attracted.
Oxygen’s valence electrons are in a higher principal energy level than nitrogen’s, so they are easier to remove.
multipleChoice.correctAnswer: In oxygen, one $$2p$$ orbital is doubly occupied, increasing electron–electron repulsion and lowering the energy needed to remove an electron.

fillInTheBlank.questionText: The approximate relationship $$Z_{\text{eff}}=Z-______$$ is used to estimate the net attraction on a valence electron.
In PES, electrons from the $$1s$$ subshell have binding energies that are ______ those from the $$2p$$ subshell.
